\chapter{The Tree}
\label{ch:ka-tree}
\hlchaptermodality{54}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a tree and its parts in Kannada, from the seed it started as to the branch at the top.}

Complete KA-C54-seed and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mara]{\kn{ಮರ} (mara) — a tree}

\label{lesson:KA-C54-tree}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{cukki} mean, and what did \emph{mōḍa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮರ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮರ}} (\emph{mara}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.

Two syllables, and one of the oldest words the family has. Tamil says \emph{maram}, Malayalam \emph{maram}, and Kannada let the closing \emph{-m} fall away, as it has a habit of doing.

\kn{ಮರ} is the standing tree and equally the wood it is cut into. A carpenter and a forester reach for the same word, and Kannada has felt no need to split them — the thing and the material are one item as far as the language is concerned.

It is also the first word of this chapter for a plain reason: everything else here is a part of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The thing the next four words belong to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mara}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{doḍḍa mara} — \textquotedblleft{}a big tree\textquotedblright{} — with the describing word in front, where Kannada keeps it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಮರ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kombe]{\kn{ಕೊಂಬೆ} (kombe) — a branch}

\label{lesson:KA-C54-branch}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mara} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕೊಂಬೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕೊಂಬೆ}} (\emph{kombe}) — \textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.

Beside it stands \kn{ಕೊಂಬು} (\emph{kombu}), a horn, and the two are the same word wearing different endings. A branch is what a \kn{ಮರ} has on its head, and the language saw an animal's horn and a tree's limb as one shape: something hard that grows outward and forks.

That picture is not a Kannada peculiarity. Tamil keeps \emph{kombu} doing both jobs as well, so the joining is old — older than any of the four sisters.

English does the reverse trick and puts the tree onto the animal, calling the branched horns of a stag its antlers and its crown. The picture travels in whichever direction a language happens to take it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the tree, and what comes out of it sideways.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kombe}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mara}, then \emph{kombe}, and say which one holds the other up
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕೊಂಬೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ele]{\kn{ಎಲೆ} (ele) — a leaf}

\label{lesson:KA-C54-leaf}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kombe} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಎಲೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎಲೆ}} (\emph{ele}) — \textquotedblleft{}a leaf\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and close to its sisters: Tamil \emph{ilai}, Malayalam \emph{ila}. Telugu is the one that walked off, using \emph{āku} instead.

The everyday weight of \kn{ಎಲೆ} is heavier than \textquotedblleft{}leaf\textquotedblright{} suggests. Say it on its own in a Kannada house and you are usually talking about the betel leaf — \kn{ಎಲೆ} \kn{ಅಡಿಕೆ}, leaf and areca nut, handed to a guest at the end of an \emph{ūṭa} and at the end of a welcome. The \kn{ಬಾಗಿಲು}, the \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ}, the \kn{ರಂಗೋಲಿ} and the \kn{ಹೂಮಾಲೆ} each had their moment; the \kn{ಎಲೆ} is what the visitor is holding on the way out.

The other big \kn{ಎಲೆ} is the plantain leaf a meal is served on, which is a plate you do not wash.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one is handed to people.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ele}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{hasiru ele} — \textquotedblleft{}a green leaf\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{ele}, \emph{kombe}, \emph{mara} upward in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಎಲೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a leaf\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bēru]{\kn{ಬೇರು} (bēru) — a root}

\label{lesson:KA-C54-root}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ele} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೇರು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೇರು}} (\emph{bēru}) — \textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.

Tamil says \emph{vēr}, Malayalam says \emph{vēr}, Telugu says \emph{vēru} — and Kannada says \kn{ಬೇರು}. That opening \emph{b} against everybody else's \emph{v} is the trade you have watched at the \kn{ಬಾಗಿಲು} and again in \kn{ಬರೆ}, and here it is once more with the letters lined up so plainly that you can hear the law rather than be told about it.

Two sound laws now separate Kannada from its sisters, and both of them are visible in a single chapter: the \emph{p} that became \emph{h} in \kn{ಹಣ್ಣು} and \kn{ಹೂವು}, and the \emph{v} that became \emph{b} in this word.

\kn{ಬೇರು} also does the figurative work English gives \emph{roots}: where a family comes from, what a word descends from. Both languages dug the same hole.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the lowest one shows the law.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bēru}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bēru}, then \emph{bāgilu}, and hear the same \emph{b} opening both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೇರು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bīja]{\kn{ಬೀಜ} (bīja) — a seed}

\label{lesson:KA-C54-seed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bēru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೀಜ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೀಜ}} (\emph{bīja}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.

Four inherited words, and then this one, straight out of Sanskrit and unaltered. The chapter closes on a borrowing, which is a fair picture of the language: the tree is Dravidian from the \kn{ಬೇರು} up, and the word for what starts it came from elsewhere.

Kannada kept its own word for the act, though. \kn{ಬಿತ್ತು} (\emph{bittu}) is to sow, and it is as native as \kn{ಮರ}. So a \kn{ರೈತ} sows with an inherited word and names what he is sowing with a borrowed one, in the same breath and without noticing.

\kn{ಬೀಜ} also does the abstract job — the seed of a quarrel, the seed of an idea — in Kannada exactly as in English, and it was doing it in Sanskrit long before either.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಮರ}, \kn{ಕೊಂಬೆ}, \kn{ಎಲೆ}, \kn{ಬೇರು}, \kn{ಬೀಜ}. A tree from the ground up, and the thing it began as.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bīja}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say which one of them Kannada borrowed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೀಜ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
